newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS opens Nazi gold archives as pledged.
newsitem.headline: BIS opens Nazi gold archives as pledged.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), central bank to the world's central banks, fulfilled a promise on Monday to open its sealed archives for research into its role in moving Nazi German gold.

The bank said its wartime records would be open to the public at its Basle headquarters from July 8, a step it had promised last month in a bid to defuse controversy over its role in the transfer of looted Nazi gold.
"The documents are open to the public," an official of the BIS's historical archive service told reporters.
The BIS released a detailed audit in May of its wartime gold dealings that confirmed earlier statements that it had handled 13.5 tonnes of gold from Hitler's Reichsbank between 1939 and 1945.
Its role was to transfer the gold, most of which was for German reparation payments from World War One, from Germany to other central banks. The BIS did not keep the gold on its own account.
Following World War Two, the BIS turned over 3.7 tonnes of gold to the Allies after the bars were identified as looted from the central banks of Belgium, Italy and the Netherlands.

The BIS sped up the planned opening of its archives after controversy about Switzerland's role as a gold buyer from Nazi Germany revived interest in the BIS' actions as an independent international institution on Swiss territory.
The wartime archives were opened first. They will be followed by all other records older than 30 years, which will be made available from early 1998.
Documents now viewable on microfilm include records of wartime gold and policy operations of member central banks from around Europe and the United States.
They also include detailed BIS gold account statements and personal files of top BIS executives before, during and shortly after the war.
